_comment: Content spec for `python manage.py seed_bulk`. Edit freely — it is data.
This is NOT a Django fixture and must not be loaded with `loaddata`. It holds
only the things a human authored: topics, banks, questions, quiz outlines,
classes. Everything derived — students, enrolments, assignments, attempts,
answers, feedback — is generated by the command through the ORM, because
`loaddata` bypasses model save() hooks and AnswerResponse's snapshot fields
A choice is [text, is_correct, explanation]. Only incorrect choices carry an
explanation: that asymmetry is why Choice.feedback_text is never exposed to a
student before they submit — the empty one would identify the answer.
`difficulty` is 0.0 (everyone gets it) to 1.0 (almost nobody does) and only
affects generated attempts. Leave it off for the 0.5 default.

topics.name: Computer Hardware
topics.description: Input, output and storage devices for the year 5 syllabus.

questions.text: What kind of device is a microphone?
choices: Input device
Output device
Output is wrong: a microphone captures sound rather than producing it.
Storage device
A microphone stores nothing — the recording is written by the computer afterwards.
Input/output device
It only sends data one way, into the computer, so it is input alone.

questions.text: Which of these is an output device?
choices: Speaker
Keyboard
A keyboard sends your keystrokes into the computer, which makes it input.
Scanner
A scanner turns paper into data for the computer, so it is an input device.
Webcam
A webcam feeds pictures into the computer rather than displaying them.

questions.text: A touchscreen is best described as which kind of device?
choices: Input/output device
Input device only
It does take your taps as input, but it also shows the picture — that is output too.
Output device only
It does display the picture, but it also senses where you touched.
Storage device
Nothing is kept on the screen; it shows what the computer sends it, moment to moment.

questions.text: Which device would you use to get a printed photograph into a computer?
choices: Scanner
Printer
A printer goes the other way — it puts what is on the computer onto paper.
Plotter
A plotter draws on paper. Like a printer, it is an output device.
Monitor
A monitor only displays; it cannot read anything from paper.

questions.text: A printer is an input device.
choices: False
True
A printer receives data from the computer and produces paper, which makes it output.

questions.text: Which of these would a blind user most likely rely on as an output device?
choices: Braille display
Trackpad
A trackpad reports where a finger moves, so it is an input device.
Barcode reader
A barcode reader feeds numbers into the computer; nothing comes out of it.
Graphics tablet
A graphics tablet captures drawing movements, which makes it input.

questions.text: Which type of memory loses its contents when the computer is switched off?
choices: RAM
ROM
ROM keeps its contents without power — that is why the start-up instructions live there.
Hard disk
A hard disk is exactly the opposite: it is where things are kept between sessions.
SSD
An SSD keeps data without power, which is why it can replace a hard disk.

questions.text: Which unit is the largest?
choices: Gigabyte
Megabyte
A megabyte is a thousand times smaller than a gigabyte.
Kilobyte
A kilobyte is the smallest of these — about a page of plain text.
Byte
A byte is a single character. Everything else here is far bigger.

questions.text: Why is an SSD usually faster than a hard disk drive?
choices: It has no moving parts to wait for
It is physically smaller
Size is not what makes it quick — plenty of small drives are slow.
It holds less data
Capacity and speed are separate things; large SSDs are fast too.
It is plugged in with a different cable
The connector matters a little, but the real reason is that nothing has to spin.

questions.text: Where does a program have to be before the processor can run it?
choices: In RAM
On the hard disk
It is stored there, but it has to be copied into memory before it can run.
In ROM
ROM holds the fixed start-up instructions, not the programs you install.
On a USB stick
A USB stick is just another place to keep the file; it still has to be loaded first.

questions.text: Backing up means keeping a second copy somewhere else.
choices: True
False
A backup is precisely a spare copy kept apart, so that one failure cannot lose both.

questions.text: Roughly how many megabytes are in a gigabyte?
choices: That is out by a factor of ten — each step up the scale multiplies by about a thousand.
Far too few. Ten megabytes is a single photograph.
That is how many kilobytes are in a gigabyte, not megabytes.

questions.text: What does the CPU do?
choices: Carries out the instructions in a program
Stores your files permanently
That is the drive's job. The processor works on data, it does not keep it.
Displays the picture on screen
The graphics chip and the monitor do that between them.
Connects the computer to the internet
That is the network card's job.

questions.text: What is the motherboard for?
choices: Connecting the components so they can talk to each other
Doing the calculations
Calculations happen in the processor, which plugs into the motherboard.
Storing the operating system
The operating system lives on a drive, not on the board itself.
Cooling the computer
Cooling is done by fans and heatsinks fitted on top of the components.

questions.text: Which component would you upgrade first if a computer runs out of memory with several programs open?
choices: RAM
CPU
A faster processor will not help if there is nowhere to put the programs while they run.
Monitor
The screen has nothing to do with how many programs fit in memory.
Keyboard
Input devices do not affect how much the computer can hold at once.

questions.text: What is the power supply unit's job?
choices: Turning mains electricity into the low voltages the parts need
Storing charge so the computer keeps running
That is a battery or a UPS. The PSU only converts, it does not store.
Cooling the processor
It has a fan of its own, but cooling the processor is the heatsink's job.
Distributing data between components
Data moves along the motherboard; the PSU carries power only.

questions.text: A graphics card is only useful for playing games.
choices: False
True
Video editing, design work and even ordinary window drawing all lean on the graphics card.

questions.text: Why do processors need a heatsink and fan?
choices: They produce heat that would otherwise damage them
They need warming up before they work
The opposite — a processor works fine cold and fails when it gets too hot.
To keep dust out of the case
A fan actually pulls dust in; filters are what keep it out.
To make the computer quieter
A fan adds noise. It is fitted despite that, because the heat has to go somewhere.

topics.name: Computer Networks
topics.description: How machines talk to each other, and how to stay safe while they do.

questions.text: What does LAN stand for?
choices: Local Area Network
Large Area Network
Size is not what the L means — a LAN is defined by being in one place.
Linked Access Node
That is not a networking term at all.
Long Alternate Network
The word is local: one building or site.

questions.text: Which device joins two different networks together?
choices: Router
Switch
A switch connects machines within one network; it does not cross between networks.
Hub
A hub repeats signals to everything plugged into it, inside a single network.
Repeater
A repeater strengthens a signal so it can travel further, on the same network.

questions.text: What is a network's main advantage over standalone computers?
choices: Files and devices can be shared
Each computer runs faster
Joining a network does not speed up the machines themselves.
Less electricity is used
A network needs extra equipment, so it usually uses a little more.
No software is needed
Networked machines still need all their usual software.

questions.text: Wi-Fi is a type of wired connection.
choices: False
True
Wi-Fi is wireless — that is the whole point of it. Ethernet is the wired one.

questions.text: Which is usually more reliable for a desktop computer that never moves?
choices: A wired Ethernet cable
Wi-Fi
Wi-Fi is convenient but shares the air with everything else nearby, so it drops more often.
Bluetooth
Bluetooth is for short-range accessories, not for connecting to a network.
Mobile data
Mobile data suits things that move; it is slower and usually metered.

questions.text: What is an IP address for?
choices: Identifying a device on a network
Storing a web page
Pages are stored on servers; the address only says which machine to ask.
Encrypting a message
Encryption is done by protocols like HTTPS, not by the address.
Measuring connection speed
Speed is measured separately; the address says where, not how fast.

questions.text: What does a web browser do?
choices: Requests web pages and displays them
Stores every web page in the world
No single machine holds the web; the browser fetches pages as you ask for them.
Creates websites automatically
Websites are written by people; the browser only shows the result.
Connects the computer to electricity
That is nothing to do with software.

questions.text: What is a search engine?
choices: A service that indexes pages so you can find them
The part of the browser that draws the page
That is the rendering engine — a different thing with a confusingly similar name.
A program that speeds up your connection
Searching and connection speed are unrelated.
The cable that carries internet traffic
Cables carry the signal; the searching happens on servers.

questions.text: The internet and the world wide web are the same thing.
choices: False
True
The internet is the network itself. The web is one of the things that runs on it, alongside email and video calls.

questions.text: What does a URL tell the browser?
choices: Where to find a particular page
How fast to load the page
Speed depends on the connection and the server, not on the address.
Who wrote the page
The address may hint at it, but nothing in a URL guarantees an author.
Whether the page is true
No address can tell you that — judging a source is your job.

questions.text: Why can the same website load quickly in one country and slowly in another?
choices: The data has further to travel and more equipment to pass through
Websites are rewritten for each country
The page is usually identical; it is the journey that differs.
Browsers work differently abroad
A browser behaves the same wherever it is run.
The time zone changes the speed
Clocks have nothing to do with it, though busy periods can.

questions.text: What is cloud storage, in plain terms?
choices: Files kept on someone else's computer, reached over the internet
Files kept in the air rather than on a disk
There is nothing airborne about it — the word cloud is just a picture.
A backup made onto a second hard disk in your own machine
That is a local backup. Cloud storage is somewhere else entirely.
Storage that never fills up
Cloud storage has limits like any other; you simply rent more.

questions.text: What makes a strong password?
choices: Long, and not used anywhere else
Your name and year of birth
Anything someone can look up about you is the first thing that gets tried.
A single dictionary word
Whole dictionaries get tested in seconds, so one word never holds.
The same one everywhere so you remember it
One leak then opens every account you own.

questions.text: What is phishing?
choices: A message pretending to be someone you trust, to get your details
A program that deletes your files
That is closer to malware. Phishing works by tricking the person, not the machine.
Slowing a website by flooding it
That is a denial of service attack, which does not involve deceiving you.
Copying software without paying
That is piracy — a different problem entirely.

questions.text: What does the padlock in the address bar mean?
choices: Traffic to that site is encrypted
The site is trustworthy
It says the connection is private, not that the people running it are honest.
The site cannot be hacked
Encryption protects the journey; it says nothing about the site's own security.
Your password is stored safely
How they store it is their business, and the padlock cannot tell you.

questions.text: You should share your password with a close friend so they can help you.
choices: False
True
A password stops being yours the moment someone else knows it, however much you trust them.

questions.text: Why is two-factor authentication useful?
choices: A stolen password alone is no longer enough to get in
It makes your password longer
The password is unchanged; the second factor is separate from it.
It encrypts your files
It controls who can sign in. Encryption is a different protection.
It stops the site being attacked
It protects your account, not the site as a whole.

questions.text: What should you do if a message urgently demands you click a link to keep your account?
choices: Ignore the link and go to the site yourself
Click quickly before the deadline
Manufactured urgency is the oldest trick in the book — it exists to stop you thinking.
Reply asking if it is genuine
Whoever sent it will happily say yes. Ask through a channel you already trust.
Forward it to your friends to warn them
Spreading it further does more harm than good; report it instead.

topics.name: Fractions & Decimals
topics.description: Year 6 number work: comparing, combining and converting.

questions.text: Which fraction is largest?
choices: Close, but 2/3 is about 0.67 and 3/4 is 0.75.
5/8 is 0.625 — smaller than both 2/3 and 3/4.
A half is the smallest here; every other option is more than half.

questions.text: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/4?
choices: Halving both parts of 2/4 gives 1/2, not 2/3.
3/4 is bigger than a half; 2/4 is exactly a half.
4/8 is also a half, but 1/2 is the simplest form asked for.

questions.text: What is 3/5 as a decimal?
choices: That is reading the digits off rather than dividing 3 by 5.
Same mistake the other way round — the digits are not the answer.
That is 5 divided by 3. The fraction bar means top divided by bottom.

questions.text: Which is the correct way to compare 3/7 and 4/9?
choices: Give them a common denominator, then compare the numerators
Compare the numerators only
3 is less than 4, but that ignores the different sized pieces.
Compare the denominators only
A bigger denominator means smaller pieces, so it cannot be read on its own.
Add the numerator and denominator of each
That produces a number with no meaning — 10 against 13 says nothing.

questions.text: A fraction with a larger denominator is always larger.
choices: False
True
A larger denominator means the pieces are smaller — 1/8 is less than 1/4, not more.

questions.text: What is 7/10 written as a percentage?
choices: That is the numerator on its own; it needs to be out of a hundred.
0.7 is the decimal. Turning it into a percentage multiplies by a hundred.
The 1 has come from nowhere — nothing in 7/10 produces it.

questions.text: What is 1/4 + 1/4?
choices: The denominators were added as well. Only the numerators combine when the bottoms match.
That is a quarter of a half — adding makes the total bigger, not smaller.
Correct as a total, but it simplifies to 1/2, which is what was asked for.

questions.text: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
choices: The tops and bottoms have each been added. Fractions need a common denominator first.
Adding cannot give less than either fraction you started with.
That is a third. The two halves of the sum have gone missing.

questions.text: Before adding 2/3 and 1/4, what has to happen?
choices: Rewrite both with the same denominator
Multiply the two numerators
That is what you do to multiply fractions, not to add them.
Turn both into whole numbers
Neither is a whole number, and rounding would lose the answer.
Subtract the smaller from the larger
That answers a different question altogether.

questions.text: What is 3/4 − 1/2?
choices: Subtracting makes the answer smaller, and 2/2 is a whole one.
That is what you took away, not what is left.
2/4 is a half. Three quarters take away two quarters leaves one.

questions.text: Adding two fractions always gives a fraction smaller than 1.
choices: False
True
3/4 + 3/4 is one and a half. Two fractions can easily pass a whole.

questions.text: What is 0.25 + 0.5?
choices: The columns have not been lined up — the 5 in 0.5 is tenths, not hundredths.
The two numbers have been written next to each other rather than added.
Close, but a quarter is 0.25, so the hundredths column still holds a 5.

questions.text: What is 0.5 as a percentage?
choices: That is 0.05. Going from a decimal to a percentage multiplies by a hundred.
The percent sign has been added without changing the number.
That is 5 whole ones — far more than a half.

questions.text: What is 25% of 80?
choices: That is the percentage itself, not a share of 80.
40 is half of 80. A quarter is half of that again.
That is 80 minus 25, which is a subtraction rather than a percentage.

questions.text: Which is the same as 0.05?
choices: 5/10 is 0.5 — ten times bigger. The extra zero moves it a column.
1/5 is 0.2. The digits look similar but the value is not.
That is 0.005, one column too far the other way.

questions.text: A shop takes 10% off a £40 coat. What do you pay?
choices: £4 is the discount, not the price after it.
That would be 25% off. Ten per cent of forty is four.
That is £1 off — 10% of £10 rather than of £40.

questions.text: Which is larger, 0.7 or 0.65?
choices: More digits does not mean more value — 0.7 is 0.70, which beats 0.65.
They are equal
0.70 and 0.65 differ by five hundredths.
It depends on rounding
Both are given exactly, so no rounding is involved.

questions.text: 100% of a number is the number itself.
choices: True
False
Per cent means out of a hundred, so a hundred out of a hundred is all of it.

topics.name: Forces & Motion
topics.description: Pushes, pulls and what happens next. Year 6 physics.

questions.text: Which force pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth?
choices: Gravity
Friction
Friction resists sliding between surfaces; it does not pull things downwards.
Air resistance
Air resistance pushes back against movement through air, in any direction.
Magnetism
Magnetism acts only on certain metals, and not everywhere on Earth.

questions.text: What is friction?
choices: A force resisting movement between two touching surfaces
A force that pulls objects together
That describes gravity or magnetism, not friction.
The weight of an object
Weight is the pull of gravity on mass; friction is separate.
The speed an object travels
Speed is a measurement, not a force.

questions.text: A force is measured in newtons.
choices: True
False
Newtons are the unit of force, named after Isaac Newton. Kilograms measure mass.

questions.text: Which of these is a contact force?
choices: Friction
Gravity
Gravity acts at a distance — the Earth pulls the Moon without touching it.
Magnetism
A magnet attracts through a gap, so it is a non-contact force.
Static electricity
A charged balloon lifts hair without touching it.

questions.text: Why does a parachute slow a falling person?
choices: It greatly increases air resistance
It reduces their weight
Their weight is unchanged; it is the upward force that grows.
It cancels gravity
Gravity still pulls just as hard. The parachute simply pushes back harder.
It makes them lighter than air
A person with a parachute is far heavier than the air around them.

questions.text: What happens when two forces on an object are balanced?
choices: Its motion does not change
It stops immediately
If it was already moving, balanced forces let it carry on at the same speed.
It speeds up
Speeding up needs an unbalanced force pushing it along.
It falls to the ground
Falling means gravity is winning, which is not balance.

questions.text: A car travels 100 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
choices: 50 km/h
200 km/h
Distance and time have been multiplied. Speed is distance divided by time.
102 km/h
The two numbers have been added, which does not give a speed.
2 km/h
That is the time, not the speed.

questions.text: Which formula gives speed?
choices: Distance divided by time
Distance multiplied by time
That grows when the journey takes longer, which is backwards.
Time divided by distance
That gives how long each kilometre takes — useful, but not speed.
Distance plus time
You cannot add a distance to a time; the units do not match.

questions.text: On a distance-time graph, what does a flat horizontal line mean?
choices: The object is not moving
The object is moving at a steady speed
Steady speed is a straight line sloping upwards, not a flat one.
The object is speeding up
Speeding up shows as a curve getting steeper.
The object is going backwards
Returning shows as a line sloping back down towards zero.

questions.text: Average speed and top speed are the same thing.
choices: False
True
A car stuck in traffic then racing along has a top speed far above its average.

questions.text: A runner covers 400 m in 50 seconds. What is the average speed?
choices: 8 m/s
The division has been done the wrong way round — that is seconds per metre.
The two numbers have been added, and the units make no sense.
Multiplying gives an impossible answer — faster than any vehicle.

questions.text: Why do we usually talk about average speed rather than speed at one moment?
choices: Real journeys speed up and slow down constantly
Instant speed cannot be measured
A speedometer does exactly that; averages are just more useful for a whole trip.
Average speed is always higher
It is usually lower than the fastest moment, not higher.
The two are the same in practice
They differ whenever the journey is not perfectly steady, which is nearly always.

questions.text: Which surface produces the most friction?
choices: Rough concrete
Polished ice
Ice is the classic low-friction surface, which is why it is slippery.
Wet tiles
Water between surfaces reduces friction, which is what makes them dangerous.
Oiled metal
Oil exists precisely to reduce friction between moving parts.

questions.text: Would you weigh more, less, or the same on the Moon?
choices: Less
More
The Moon is far smaller, so it pulls less strongly, not more.
The same
Weight depends on the pull of gravity, which differs from world to world.
Nothing at all
The Moon does have gravity — about a sixth of Earth's, not none.

questions.text: Friction is always a nuisance.
choices: False
True
Without friction you could not walk, and brakes would not work. It is often exactly what we want.

questions.text: Why do falling objects eventually stop speeding up?
choices: Air resistance grows until it balances their weight
Gravity gets weaker as they fall
Gravity barely changes over the heights we can fall from.
They run out of energy
Falling does not use anything up; the energy is being converted, not spent.
The ground pushes up before they land
The ground only pushes once they reach it.

questions.text: What is the difference between mass and weight?
choices: Mass is how much matter there is; weight is the force of gravity on it
They are the same, measured in different units
They are genuinely different quantities — mass never changes, weight does.
Weight is measured in kilograms, mass in newtons
It is the other way round: mass in kilograms, weight in newtons.
Mass changes with location
Mass is the same everywhere. It is weight that changes with gravity.

questions.text: Why do cyclists crouch low over the handlebars?
choices: To reduce air resistance
To increase their weight
Position does not change weight, and extra weight would not help.
To reduce friction with the road
Grip on the road is wanted, not avoided — without it the tyres would slip.
To pedal harder
It can help a little, but the main gain is slipping through the air.

topics.name: Photosynthesis & Plants
topics.description: Year 7 biology — how plants feed themselves.

questions.text: Which gas do plants take in to make their food?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Oxygen is what photosynthesis gives out, not what it uses up.
Nitrogen
Nitrogen is most of the air, but plants take it from the soil, not for food-making.
Hydrogen
The hydrogen a plant needs comes from water drawn up by the roots.

questions.text: What do plants produce during photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
Those are the ingredients going in, not the products coming out.
Protein and starch
Starch is made later, from the glucose; protein needs nitrogen from the soil.
Only oxygen
Oxygen is the by-product. The point of the process is the sugar.

questions.text: Where does a plant get the water for photosynthesis?
choices: From the soil, through its roots
From the air, through its leaves
Leaves take in gas, not liquid water.
It makes its own
Water is an ingredient, not a product.
From sunlight
Sunlight provides the energy; the water has to come from somewhere physical.

questions.text: Photosynthesis can happen in the dark.
choices: False
True
Light is the energy source for the whole process, so without it nothing happens.

questions.text: What is the green substance in leaves that traps light called?
choices: Chlorophyll
Chloroplast
Very close — the chloroplast is the container. Chlorophyll is the green pigment inside it.
Cellulose
Cellulose is what plant cell walls are built from; it is not green and traps no light.
Glucose
Glucose is the sugar produced at the end, not the thing that catches the light.

questions.text: Why do plants matter to animals that do not eat them?
choices: They release the oxygen animals breathe
They provide shade
Useful, but not the reason animal life depends on them.
They keep the soil warm
That is not a role plants play in any important way.
They produce carbon dioxide
They consume far more carbon dioxide than they give out.

questions.text: Why are most leaves broad and flat?
choices: To catch as much light as possible
To collect rainwater
Water is taken up by the roots, not caught by the leaves.
To make the plant look bigger
Appearance is not something a plant is shaped for.
To store food
Some plants store food in roots or stems; the leaf's shape is about light.

questions.text: What are stomata?
choices: Tiny pores that let gases in and out of a leaf
The veins carrying water through a leaf
Those are xylem vessels — a separate system inside the leaf.
The green pigment in a leaf
That is chlorophyll.
The waxy layer on top of a leaf
That is the cuticle, which keeps water in rather than letting gas through.

questions.text: Which part of a plant carries water upwards from the roots?
choices: Xylem
Phloem
Phloem carries dissolved sugar around the plant, and it travels both ways.
Stomata
Stomata handle gases at the leaf surface, not water inside the stem.
Cuticle
The cuticle is a waterproof coating; nothing travels through it.

questions.text: Leaves are usually darker green on the upper surface.
choices: True
False
The upper surface holds more chloroplasts because it receives more light.

questions.text: Why do stomata mostly sit on the underside of a leaf?
choices: It is cooler and shaded, so less water escapes
It is easier for insects to reach
Plants gain nothing from making gas exchange easier for insects.
The upper surface is too thin
The upper surface is usually thicker, with its waxy cuticle.
Gases only travel downwards
Gases diffuse in every direction equally.

questions.text: What is the waxy cuticle on a leaf for?
choices: Reducing water loss
Absorbing light
It is transparent, so light passes straight through to the cells below.
Taking in carbon dioxide
That happens through the stomata; the cuticle is a barrier.
Storing sugar
Sugar is stored in the cells, not in the surface coating.

questions.text: Which process do plants use to release energy from glucose?
choices: Respiration
Photosynthesis
Photosynthesis makes the glucose. Getting energy back out of it is respiration.
Transpiration
Transpiration is water evaporating from the leaves; no energy is released.
Digestion
Plants have no digestive system — they make their food rather than break it down.

questions.text: Do plants respire at night?
choices: Yes, all the time
No, only in daylight
That is photosynthesis. Respiration never stops, day or night.
Only when they are growing
Every living cell respires continuously, growing or not.
Only in winter
Season makes no difference to whether respiration happens.

questions.text: What is transpiration?
choices: Water evaporating from a plant's leaves
Water being taken in by the roots
That is absorption. Transpiration is the loss at the other end.
Sugar moving around the plant
That is translocation, through the phloem.
Gas exchange in the leaf
Gas exchange happens alongside it, but transpiration is about water.

questions.text: Cutting down forests reduces the amount of carbon dioxide removed from the air.
choices: True
False
Fewer trees means less photosynthesis, and it is photosynthesis that takes the gas out of the air.

questions.text: During a bright day, what does a plant do overall?
choices: Takes in more carbon dioxide than it gives out
Gives out more carbon dioxide than it takes in
That happens at night, when only respiration is running.
Neither, the two exactly cancel
They balance only at one particular light level, not through a bright day.
Stops respiring altogether
Respiration continues; photosynthesis simply outpaces it.

questions.text: What would happen to a plant kept in a sealed dark box for a week?
choices: It would use up its stored food and start to die
It would grow faster with no competition
Nothing about a dark box helps growth; light is what it lacks.
It would keep photosynthesising from stored light
Light cannot be stored — only the sugar made from it can.
It would be unaffected for months
Stored starch runs out in days to weeks, not months.

topics.name: World Geography
topics.description: Continents, rivers and weather for the year 7 syllabus.

questions.text: Which is the longest river in Africa?
choices: The Nile
The Congo
The Congo carries more water, but the Nile runs further.
The Niger
The Niger is major but considerably shorter than the Nile.
The Zambezi
The Zambezi is famous for Victoria Falls rather than for its length.

questions.text: What is the source of a river?
choices: Where it begins
Where it meets the sea
That is the mouth, at the opposite end.
The widest part
Width varies along the whole course and marks nothing in particular.
Where another river joins it
That is a confluence.

questions.text: Which mountain range separates France from Spain?
choices: The Pyrenees
The Alps
The Alps are further east, between France, Switzerland and Italy.
The Carpathians
The Carpathians curve through central and eastern Europe.
The Apennines
The Apennines run the length of Italy.

questions.text: Mount Everest is in the Andes.
choices: False
True
Everest is in the Himalayas, in Asia. The Andes run down South America.

questions.text: How are most mountain ranges formed?
choices: Tectonic plates pushing against each other
Rivers cutting the land away
Rivers carve valleys into existing high ground; they do not raise it.
Wind piling up rock
Wind moves sand into dunes, nothing on the scale of a mountain range.
Ice freezing and expanding
Ice shapes mountains once they exist, but does not create the range.

questions.text: What is a delta?
choices: A fan of channels where a river meets the sea
A deep valley cut by a river
That is a gorge or canyon, usually far upstream.
A lake at a river's source
Some rivers begin in lakes, but that is not called a delta.
A waterfall
A waterfall is a sudden drop, typically over hard rock.

questions.text: Which is the largest ocean?
choices: Pacific
Atlantic
The Atlantic is second — roughly half the Pacific's area.
Indian
The Indian Ocean is third largest.
Arctic
The Arctic is the smallest of the four.

questions.text: How many continents are usually counted?
choices: Seven
Five
Five is the count used by the Olympic rings, which leaves out the uninhabited one.
Six
Six comes from joining Europe and Asia into Eurasia, which is not the usual school count.
Eight
There is no widely used eight-continent model.

questions.text: Which continent is entirely in the southern hemisphere?
choices: Antarctica
Africa
Africa straddles the equator, so part of it is northern.
South America
Its northern tip, including Colombia, sits above the equator.
Australia
Australia is southern, but so is Antarctica — and Antarctica is the clearer answer here.

questions.text: The equator passes through Europe.
choices: False
True
Europe lies entirely north of the equator; the line crosses Africa, South America and Asia.

questions.text: Which continent has the largest population?
choices: Asia
Africa
Africa is growing fastest but is still well behind Asia in total.
Europe
Europe holds under a tenth of the world's people.
North America
North America has fewer people than Europe.

questions.text: What separates North America from Asia at their closest point?
choices: The Bering Strait
The Panama Canal
The canal cuts through Central America, joining two oceans.
The Strait of Gibraltar
That is between Spain and Morocco.
The Suez Canal
Suez separates Africa from Asia, not Asia from North America.

questions.text: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: Weather is day to day; climate is the long-term pattern
They mean the same thing
One cold week says nothing about climate, which is measured over decades.
Climate is day to day; weather is long term
That is the right idea reversed.
Weather applies to land, climate to sea
Both terms apply everywhere.

questions.text: Which instrument measures rainfall?
choices: Rain gauge
Barometer
A barometer measures air pressure.
Anemometer
An anemometer measures wind speed.
Thermometer
A thermometer measures temperature.

questions.text: Why is it colder at the top of a mountain?
choices: Air is thinner and holds heat less well
It is further from the sun
A few kilometres is nothing against 150 million — that cannot be the reason.
Snow makes it cold
The snow is there because it is cold, not the other way round.
There is more wind
Wind makes it feel colder but is not why the temperature is lower.

questions.text: Places near the equator generally have warmer climates.
choices: True
False
Sunlight arrives most directly at the equator, so those regions receive the most energy.

questions.text: What causes wind?
choices: Differences in air pressure
The Earth spinning alone
Rotation bends the wind's path, but something has to start it moving first.
Trees moving
Trees move because of the wind, not the reverse.
The tide
Tides move water, and are driven by the Moon rather than the air.

questions.text: Which of these best describes a desert climate?
choices: Very little rainfall
Always extremely hot
Antarctica is a desert, and so are parts of central Asia that freeze in winter.
Always sandy
Many deserts are rock or ice; sand dunes are a minority of desert land.
No living things
Deserts hold plenty of specially adapted plants and animals.
